text: In a cell that is not dividing, chromosomes are typically long, thin and spread out, far too fine to pick out with a light microscope. As division begins, each replicated chromosome condenses: it coils more tightly, becoming shorter and thicker, until, once stained, you can see it. That is the familiar X shape: two sister chromatids held at the centromere, with a telomere at each of the four ends.
